> Connecting points creates more complicated data types—vector data—that represent lines and polygons.

<!-- END module:header -->

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library( sf )
library( tidyverse )
theme_set( theme_minimal( base_size = 16 ) )
```

In the [points](https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/Spatial-Points/narrative.html) topic, every row of an `sf` object was a single coordinate.  Here we connect those coordinates into more complicated *vector* types: lines (`LINESTRING`) and polygons (`POLYGON` and `MULTIPOLYGON`).  They are still `sf` objects, so the same `st_*` functions and the same plotting routines (both built-in `plot()` and `ggplot()` with `geom_sf()`) work on them.

We will:

- Build `LINESTRING` and `POLYGON` objects *de novo* from a `data.frame` of coordinates.
- Make polygons from the map data that comes with `ggplot2`.
- Import real vector data from ESRI shapefiles.
- Use spatial joins to select features by *where* they are instead of by a key column.

## Lines

### Lines *de novo*

A line is just a sequence of points, connected in the order given.  So let's start with some points.  Here I make 10 random locations in central Virginia, five belonging to `Rodney` and five to `Sarah`, each with a bit of `Data` attached.

```{r}
set.seed( 543 )
df <- data.frame( id = c( rep("Rodney", 5), rep("Sarah", 5) ),
                  Data = rnorm( 10, 42, 42 ),
                  Longitude = rnorm( 10, -78, 1 ),
                  Latitude = rnorm( 10, 37, 1 ) )
df
```

Just as before, we turn these into `POINT` objects with `st_as_sf()`, telling it which columns hold the coordinates and what coordinate reference system (CRS) they are in (EPSG 4326 is plain longitude/latitude).

```{r}
df %>%
  st_as_sf( coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326 ) -> pts
pts
```

```{r}
ggplot( pts ) +
  geom_sf( aes( color = id, size = Data ) ) +
  coord_sf()
```

To make lines, we need to collapse each person's five points into a single row.  We `group_by()` the `id`, `summarize()` the `Data` column (here by its mean), which leaves a `MULTIPOINT` geometry for each group, and then `st_cast()` that collection into a `LINESTRING`.

```{r}
df %>%
  st_as_sf( coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326 ) %>%
  group_by( id ) %>%
  summarize( Data = mean( Data ) ) %>%
  st_cast( "LINESTRING" ) -> lines
lines
```

### Visualizing Lines

Just like points, we can plot these with the built-in `plot()` function, here selecting the `Data` column to plot,

```{r}
plot( lines["Data"], lwd = 2 )
```

or with `ggplot()`.

```{r}
ggplot( lines ) +
  geom_sf( aes( color = id ), linewidth = 2 ) +
  coord_sf()
```

### Operations on Lines

Because the geometry is spatially aware, we can ask spatial questions of it.  The physical length of each `LINESTRING` (in meters, since `sf` computes distances on the globe for lat/lon data):

```{r}
st_length( lines )
```

The bounding box surrounding all the lines:

```{r}
st_bbox( lines )
```

And the area of the convex hull that encloses *all* the lines.  Here I `st_union()` the two lines into one geometry, wrap a hull around it, measure its area, and use the `units` library to express it in square kilometers.

```{r}
library( units )
lines %>%
  st_union() %>%
  st_convex_hull() %>%
  st_area() %>%
  set_units( km^2 )
```

### Textual Versions of Geometry

Every geometry can also be written as *Well Known Text* (WKT), a plain-text description of the shape and its coordinates.  This is handy when you want to see exactly what a geometry contains.

```{r}
lines$geometry[1] %>% st_as_text()
```

## Polygons

A polygon is simply a line whose first and last coordinates are exactly the same, so it closes upon itself.  To see this, here are our points again with the first point of each person repeated at the end of their sequence.

```{r}
df.p <- df[ c( 1:5, 1, 6:10, 6 ), ]
df.p
```

### Polygons *de novo*

We make polygons the same way we made lines, just casting to `POLYGON` instead.  `st_cast()` closes each ring for us by repeating the first point.

```{r}
df %>%
  st_as_sf( coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326 ) %>%
  group_by( id ) %>%
  summarize( Data = mean( Data ) ) %>%
  st_cast( "POLYGON" ) -> polygons
polygons
```

```{r}
ggplot( polygons ) +
  geom_sf( aes( fill = Data ), alpha = 0.75 ) +
  coord_sf()
```

Since the points are random, the order they are connected in is random too, so these polygons may cross over themselves.  Real polygons are made from points that go around the outside of a shape in order.

### Polygons from Data Frames

For real shapes, we can grab polygon data from `ggplot` itself.  The `map_data()` function (it uses the `maps` library) returns a `data.frame` of coordinates.  Here are the counties of Virginia.

```{r}
library( maps )
map_data( "county", "virginia" ) %>%
  select( Longitude = long,
          Latitude = lat,
          group,
          County = subregion ) -> va_counties
head( va_counties )
```

To get an idea of what these data represent, let's first plot just the points.  This shows where all the coordinates are, without the connecting lines.

```{r}
ggplot( va_counties, aes( Longitude, Latitude ) ) +
  geom_point( size = 0.25 ) +
  coord_quickmap()
```

Each county is identified by its `group`.  If we look at a couple of counties, it is easier to see how the polygons are constructed: the points (in color) are connected in order to make the outline (the shaded polygon).

```{r}
va_counties %>%
  filter( County %in% c("hanover", "henrico") ) %>%
  ggplot( aes( Longitude, Latitude ) ) +
  geom_polygon( aes( fill = County ), alpha = 0.1 ) +
  geom_point( aes( color = County ) ) +
  coord_quickmap()
```

Notice that the points on the shared border are repeated in both `County == "hanover"` and `County == "henrico"`.  Each polygon is complete on its own.

Using `geom_polygon()` with `group = group` draws them all.

```{r}
ggplot( va_counties, aes( Longitude, Latitude ) ) +
  geom_polygon( aes( group = group ),
                fill = "grey80",
                color = "black",
                linewidth = 0.25 ) +
  coord_quickmap()
```

We can also layer `sf` objects on top of these.  Here are the lines we made earlier on top of the counties.  Notice that we use `coord_sf()` here, since we are now mixing in an `sf` layer.

```{r}
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon( aes( Longitude, Latitude, group = group ),
                fill = "grey80",
                color = "black",
                linewidth = 0.25,
                data = va_counties ) +
  geom_sf( aes( color = Data ),
           linewidth = 2,
           data = lines ) +
  coord_sf()
```

## Shapefiles

Most of the time we are not going to make vector data by hand; we will load it from a file someone else created.  A very common format for this is the ESRI *shapefile*, which can hold `POINT`, `LINESTRING`, `POLYGON` and other vector types.

The first thing to understand is that *a shapefile* is not an actual file.  It is a collection of several files with the same name and different extensions, and they are usually zipped up into a single archive.

### Downloading the Archives

For this topic we will use roads and zoning districts for Richmond, Virginia, made available by the GIS Department of the City of Richmond.  Here are the two archives in the [course data repository](https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/CourseData/).

```{r}
roads_url <- "https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/CourseData/Spatial/Richmond_Roads.zip"
district_url <- "https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/CourseData/Spatial/Richmond_ZoningDistricts.zip"
```

You can download them with your browser and move them into your project folder, or you can have `R` download them.  The `destfile` argument says where to save each archive.  Here I put them in a temporary folder (`tempdir()`) so the raw files do not clutter up the project, but on your own computer you will usually save them into a `data` folder in your project (e.g., `destfile = "data/Roads.zip"`) so you only have to download them once.

```{r}
shp_dir <- tempdir()
download.file( roads_url, destfile = file.path( shp_dir, "Roads.zip" ) )
download.file( district_url, destfile = file.path( shp_dir, "Districts.zip" ) )
```

### Unzipping

Before we can use them, we need to unzip them.  You can do this in your computer's file browser, or have `R` do it.  The `exdir` argument tells `unzip()` where to put the expanded files.

```{r}
unzip( file.path( shp_dir, "Roads.zip" ), exdir = shp_dir )
unzip( file.path( shp_dir, "Districts.zip" ), exdir = shp_dir )
```

Depending upon how the archives were created, they may expand into a subfolder or just put a pile of files in the same folder.  For this example, there is one of each: the `Zoning_Districts.*` files are expanded directly into the folder and the roads are expanded into a subfolder named `Centerlines-shp`.

![The expanded shapefile components: five `Zoning_Districts` files and the `Centerlines-shp` folder.](media/flickr_50540213032.jpg){fig-alt="A file listing showing Zoning_Districts.cpg, .dbf, .prj, .shp, and .shx files, and a folder named Centerlines-shp."}

```{r}
list.files( shp_dir, recursive = TRUE, pattern = "Zoning|tran_" )
```

### File Components

Each of these files holds one part of the data set:

- `.shp` holds the geometry (the coordinates of each feature).
- `.shx` is an index into the geometry, so features can be found quickly.
- `.dbf` holds the attribute table (the non-spatial columns for each feature).
- `.prj` holds the projection, the coordinate reference system the coordinates are in.
- `.cpg` gives the character encoding used in the `.dbf` file.

The `.prj` file is plain text.  If you open it, you will see the full definition of the projection.

![The contents of `Zoning_Districts.prj`, describing the NAD83 Virginia South (US feet) projection.](media/flickr_50540256782.jpg){fig-alt="A text editor showing the Zoning_Districts.prj file, which defines the NAD83 Virginia South ftUS projection using a Lambert Conformal Conic projection with units of US feet."}

### Loading a Shapefile

To load a shapefile, we use `st_read()` and pass it the path to the `.shp` file.  It finds the other component files on its own.

```{r}
districts <- st_read( file.path( shp_dir, "Zoning_Districts.shp" ) )
```

The result is an `sf` object.  The attributes from the `.dbf` file are put into the `data.frame` and the `geometry` column is built from the `.shp` file.  Each row here is a `MULTIPOLYGON`.

```{r}
class( districts )
head( districts, n = 2 )
```

Notice the projection: `NAD83 / Virginia South (ftUS)`.  If you look it up on [epsg.io](https://epsg.io/2284), it is EPSG 2284, and its units are US feet, not degrees.

### Simplifying the Data

There are a lot of columns here, many of which are bookkeeping from the GIS department.

```{r}
names( districts )
```

Let's drop the ones we do not need.  `Shape__Are` and `Shape__Len` are the area and perimeter of each polygon, which we can always recalculate with `st_area()` and `st_perimeter()`.

```{r}
districts %>%
  select( -Comment, -CreatedBy, -CreatedDat, -EditBy, -EditDate ) %>%
  select( -Shape__Are, -Shape__Len ) -> districts
head( districts, n = 1 )
```

The `Name` column holds the zoning code for each district.

```{r}
districts$Name %>% unique() %>% sort()
```

### Visualizing

We can plot it normally using `plot()` for `sf` objects, coloring by zoning code,

```{r}
plot( districts["Name"] )
```

and we can overlay one district on top of all of them by plotting just the geometry (`st_geometry()`) and then adding a second layer with `add = TRUE`.

```{r}
plot( st_geometry( districts ) )
plot( st_geometry( districts[ districts$OBJECTID == 530, ] ),
      col = "red",
      add = TRUE )
```

## Vector Operations

In the [Joins](https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/Joins/narrative.html) topic, we used primary and foreign keys to join `data.frame` objects together.  With spatial data, we can also combine data sets using their *positions*: which features intersect, touch, contain, or are within some distance of each other.  These are called *spatial joins*, and there are a lot of them.  Check out the [`sf` cheatsheet](https://github.com/rstudio/cheatsheets/blob/main/sf.pdf) for the full list.

### A Second Data Set

Let's load in the roads.  This shapefile was in the `Centerlines-shp` subfolder.

```{r}
road.shapefile <- st_read( file.path( shp_dir, "Centerlines-shp/tran_Carriageway.shp" ) )
names( road.shapefile )
```

Each of the `r nrow( road.shapefile )` rows is a `LINESTRING` representing one segment of road.

### Check Projections

Before combining two spatial data sets, you must make sure they are in the same projection[^1].

```{r}
st_crs( road.shapefile ) == st_crs( districts )
```

These are both from the same GIS department, so they match.  If they differed, we would reproject one to match the other with `st_transform()`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
road.shapefile %>%
  st_transform( crs = st_crs( districts ) ) -> road.shapefile
```

### Data Cleanup

Let's keep only the columns we need, rename a couple of the abbreviated ones, and make the categorical columns into factors.

```{r}
road.shapefile %>%
  select( FullName, OneWay, StreetType,
          SpeedLimit = PostedSpee,
          Length = SHAPE_Leng,
          geometry ) %>%
  mutate( OneWay = factor( OneWay ),
          StreetType = factor( StreetType ) ) -> roads
summary( roads )
```

### Filtering and Plotting Lines

Since `roads` is a `data.frame`, we can use normal `dplyr` routines on it.  Here I grab just the highways, interchanges, and ramps,

```{r}
roads %>%
  filter( StreetType %in% c("Highway",
                            "Highway Interchange",
                            "Ramp") ) -> highways
summary( highways )
```

and plot them colored by speed limit.

```{r}
plot( highways["SpeedLimit"], lwd = 4 )
```

For any particular street, say *Three Chopt Road*, we can filter out the rows for it.

```{r}
roads %>%
  filter( FullName == "Three Chopt Road" ) -> three_chopt
nrow( three_chopt )
```

The road is made of `r nrow( three_chopt )` separate `LINESTRING` segments.  Each one is a sequence of points, which we can see as text,

```{r}
three_chopt$geometry[1] %>% st_as_text()
```

or plot all of them together.

```{r}
ggplot( three_chopt ) +
  geom_sf( aes( color = SpeedLimit ), linewidth = 2 ) +
  coord_sf()
```

### Cropping to The Fan

Let's focus on the area around VCU and *The Fan*.  The large residential district in the middle of the Fan is `OBJECTID == 368`.  To get a region around it, I buffer that polygon by 1500 feet (the units of this projection), take the bounding box of the result, and then crop all the districts to that box.

```{r}
districts %>%
  filter( OBJECTID == 368 ) %>%
  st_buffer( dist = 1500 ) %>%
  st_bbox() -> fan_bbox

districts %>%
  st_crop( fan_bbox ) -> theFan
plot( theFan["Name"] )
```

`st_crop()` will warn you that it assumes the attributes are the same across each geometry.  That just means that when it cuts a district in half at the edge of the box, the half it keeps gets all the original attributes, which is what we want.

### Adding Auxiliary Data

The zoning codes are not very descriptive.  There is a csv file with a translation in the course data repository, and we can `left_join()` it to `theFan` by the `Name` column as it is read in[^2].

```{r}
zone_url <- "https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/CourseData/Spatial/Richmond_ZoningCodes.csv"

theFan %>%
  left_join( read_csv( zone_url ),
             by = "Name" ) %>%
  mutate( Category = factor( Category ) ) %>%
  select( OBJECTID,
          Name,
          Category,
          everything() ) -> theFan
```

```{r}
ggplot( theFan ) +
  geom_sf( aes( fill = Category ) ) +
  scale_fill_brewer( type = "qual",
                     palette = "Set3" )
```

Notice that `geom_sf()` draws the axes in longitude and latitude, even though the data are in feet.  It converts the coordinates for display without changing the data.

### Cropping the Roads

We can crop the roads to the same box.

```{r}
roads %>%
  st_crop( st_bbox( theFan ) ) -> fanRoads
plot( st_geometry( theFan ), lwd = 2 )
plot( st_geometry( fanRoads ), col = "blue", add = TRUE )
```

### Selecting a Single Zone

Let's mark the target district in `theFan` with a new column, and plot it with each district's `OBJECTID` as a label so we can see which one it is.

```{r}
theFan %>%
  mutate( Target = OBJECTID == 368 ) -> theFan

theFan %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf( aes( fill = Target ) ) +
  geom_sf_text( aes( label = OBJECTID ), size = 3 ) +
  coord_sf()
```

And then pull it out as its own `sf` object.

```{r}
target <- theFan %>% filter( OBJECTID == 368 )
plot( st_geometry( target ) )
```

### Spatial Joins

Now for the question we have been building toward: *which roads cross this district?*  The `st_filter()` function keeps the rows of one `sf` object that satisfy a spatial relationship with another.  By default, that relationship is `st_intersects()`, meaning they share at least one point.

```{r}
fanRoads %>%
  st_filter( target ) -> targetRoads
nrow( targetRoads )
```

Those are `r nrow( targetRoads )` road segments.  To get the street names, we drop the geometry with `st_drop_geometry()` (otherwise the `geometry` column comes along for the ride) and use normal `dplyr` routines.

```{r}
targetRoads %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select( `Street Name` = FullName ) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  arrange( `Street Name` )
```

And we can plot them on top of the districts, with the target highlighted.

```{r}
ggplot() +
  geom_sf( aes( fill = Target ), data = theFan ) +
  geom_sf( color = "darkgreen", data = targetRoads ) +
  scale_fill_manual( values = c("grey90", "dodgerblue3") )
```

To use a different relationship, pass it as the `.predicate`.  For example, `st_filter( fanRoads, target, .predicate = st_within )` would keep only the road segments that lie *completely* inside the district.  Go check out the `sf` cheatsheet for more spatial joins and options.

[^1]: **Dyer's First Law**: Reproject then forget about it!

[^2]: You should be careful when you use joins on `sf` objects.  If your `sf` object is on the right side (see discussion of joins [here](https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/Joins/narrative.html)) then the result will not be an `sf` object and you'll have to coerce it back into one again.  It always adopts the characteristics of the left object.
